bull_bear.body: Confident but candid. Repeatedly stressed "resilience," "highest ever revenue," and net-cash balance sheet. bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Macroeconomic and geopolitical environment — BRSR material-issue risk: changes in the global economic environment, financial market conditions and adverse geopolitical developments may impact the Group's revenue and profitability. Demand for refractory products is directly influenced by steel, cement, glass and non-ferrous metal production, so sales-volume fluctuations feed straight into capacity utilisation, profitability and gearing. Flagged with negative financial implications.
- Demand cyclicality and commoditisation pressure from customer end-markets — Specific risks flagged include decreasing investment and delays in customers' infrastructure projects reducing steel and cement demand, customers shifting to lower-cost and more commoditised refractories because of low capacity utilisation, and lower sales volumes leading to poorer fixed-cost absorption. The Indian refractory industry is separately described as facing excess capacity, pricing pressure and increasing commoditisation of standard products.
- Input cost inflation, tariffs and currency exposure — Increasing costs of core resources and supplies (energy, labour, raw materials, freight, packaging), increased trade restrictions, tariffs or export bans that could disrupt supply chains and raise material costs, and currency fluctuations affecting the cost of imports and exports. Mitigation relies on price-increase initiatives to pass inflationary costs to customers and treasury policy.
- Production network and supply-chain disruption — BRSR material-issue risk covering structural weakness in the production network, production interruption at a single-source manufacturing site, inability to accurately predict customer demand leading to missed sales and inefficient production planning, global logistics challenges, and natural disaster or major political crisis in one or more regions. Mitigated by geographical diversification of the production network and minimisation of sole-source materials.
- Regulatory and compliance risk, including bribery and corruption exposure — BRSR material-issue risk: the Company faces increasing regulatory complexity and operates in some geographies with inherently high corruption risks. Specific risks flagged include failure to act in accordance with the Code of Conduct, violation of anti-bribery and corruption laws by employees or third-party representatives, violation of data privacy and AI regulations, and violation of anti-trust regulations. Flagged with negative financial implications.
- Human rights and labour standards — BRSR material-issue risk: failing to maintain safe, equitable and fair labour conditions across localised workforces or value chains results in severe legal liabilities, workplace friction or negative community impacts. Flagged with negative financial implications.
- Concentration of business with related parties — BRSR concentration disclosure shows related-party transactions form a material share of both purchases and sales, and that investments in related parties dominate total investments, leaving the Company structurally dependent on the RHI Magnesita Group for sourcing, offtake and capital deployment.
- Global steel overcapacity and Chinese export-driven price pressure — Management describes the global steel industry as under pressure from persistent overcapacity, weak steel prices and rising trade protectionism, with China dominating global steel exports and driving elevated pricing pressure plus an increase in antidumping duties and safeguard measures across several markets — a structural headwind for the customer base that consumes refractories.

- Diversify beyond steel through the Industrial Division into cement, lime, chemicals, glass, energy, petrochemicals and non-ferrous industries, which offer higher value-added product opportunities and better margin profiles, reducing sectoral concentration risk.
- Build circular-economy and low-carbon capability through increased recycling and sustainable refractory solutions aligned with the evolving green steel and low-carbon industrial ecosystem.
- Reinforce an industry-leading safety culture through structured safety programs supported by DSS+ operational consultants across manufacturing locations.
- Grow inorganically and integrate acquisitions, having added Dalmia Bharat Refractories, Hi-Tech Chemicals and Ashwath Technologies domestically and benefited from group-level acquisitions of Seven Refractories, PD Refractories and RESCO.

outlook.body: RHIM India operates 8 strategically located manufacturing plants, 2 mines and 2 mechanism plants, with an installed manufacturing capacity of 512 kt and ongoing expansion plans, positioning it to address both domestic and export demand while drawing on the RHI Magnesita Group's global production network. Expansion during FY 2025-26 came primarily through inorganic and capability additions rather than named greenfield projects: Ashwath Technologies Private Limited became a step-down subsidiary with effect from August 1, 2025 and its integration progressed during the year, strengthening the customer base in the mini mills steel segment and enhancing offerings across slide gate systems, spare parts, refractory resale and steel flow control machinery; RHI Magnesita Seven Refractories Limited was merged into RHI Magnesita India Refractories Limited. The Company also cites domestic acquisitions of Dalmia Bharat Refractories, Hi-Tech Chemicals and Ashwath Technologies as having expanded capacity and diversified capabilities, and global acquisitions of Seven Refractories, PD Refractories and RESCO as having strengthened range, efficiency and technological depth. Manufacturing capability was further built out through technology transfer to local plants, localisation of advanced products, automation initiatives and increased recycling. R&D investment at the Bhiwadi, Rajasthan centre added world-class equipment including advanced thermal conductivity testing systems, viscometers, a new pilot Eirich mixer, high temperature furnaces and hot MOR facilities. Approximately 2% of total capital expenditure during FY 2025-26 was attributable to environmental, occupational health and safety and social projects, including sewage and effluent treatment upgrades, rainwater recharge pits, dust collection systems and sanitation facilities for women employees.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Refractory demand is directly linked to steel, cement, glass and non-ferrous metal production; steel accounts for nearly 70% of total refractory consumption in India.
- India's steelmaking capacity rose to approximately 220 MT during FY 2025-26 and remains on track towards the National Steel Policy target of 300 MT by 2030-31, with cumulative investments of approximately US$ 156 billion expected to achieve it.
- India remained the world's second-largest crude steel producer, with crude steel production of 153.6 MT and finished steel production of 146.8 MT in April 2025-February 2026, and turned a net exporter with a surplus of 0.40 MT versus a net import position in FY 2024-25.
- Indian cement production reached approximately 485 million tonnes in FY 2025-26, growing nearly 8.0%-9.0% YoY, with planned industry capital expenditure of approximately Rs 1.2-1.25 lakh crore across FY 2024-25 to FY 2026-27 toward capacity additions of nearly 130-170 MTPA; the long-term outlook for cement remains favourable through FY 2027-28.
- India's real GDP was projected to expand by approximately 7.6% in FY 2025-26, with roughly 70% of economic activity from domestic demand, supporting core industries including refractories.
- The global refractories market was valued at approximately USD 38-48 billion in 2025, with volumes rising from approximately 57 million tons in 2025 to nearly 59.6 million tons in 2026 and projected to reach around 72 million tons by 2031 at a CAGR of approximately 3.9%-4.0%; Asia-Pacific dominates the market.
- Green steel and decarbonisation momentum in India is expected to create long-term opportunities for advanced, sustainable and technology-driven refractory solutions.
- Increasing adoption of electric vehicles, renewable energy and critical metal processing is expected to further drive demand for advanced refractory solutions in the coming years.
- Headwind: the global steel industry remained under pressure from persistent overcapacity — global steelmaking capacity reached an estimated 2.6 billion metric tons by end-2025 with surplus capacity of approximately 680 million metric tons — plus weak prices, Chinese export dominance and rising trade protectionism.
- Headwind: the Indian refractory industry continues to face excess capacity, pricing pressure and increasing commoditisation of standard refractory products.
- Industrials contributed approximately 13% of RHIM India's revenues during the year, providing diversification while steel remains the largest revenue driver; the Industrial business gained market share across select segments.

risks.note: BRSR material-issue risk: changes in the global economic environment, financial market conditions and adverse geopolitical developments may impact the Group's revenue and profitability. Demand for refractory products is directly influenced by steel, cement, glass and non-ferrous metal production, so sales-volume fluctuations feed straight into capacity utilisation, profitability and gearing. Flagged with negative financial implications.

Specific risks flagged include decreasing investment and delays in customers' infrastructure projects reducing steel and cement demand, customers shifting to lower-cost and more commoditised refractories because of low capacity utilisation, and lower sales volumes leading to poorer fixed-cost absorption. The Indian refractory industry is separately described as facing excess capacity, pricing pressure and increasing commoditisation of standard products.
risks.risk: Demand cyclicality and commoditisation pressure from customer end-markets

risks.note: Increasing costs of core resources and supplies (energy, labour, raw materials, freight, packaging), increased trade restrictions, tariffs or export bans that could disrupt supply chains and raise material costs, and currency fluctuations affecting the cost of imports and exports. Mitigation relies on price-increase initiatives to pass inflationary costs to customers and treasury policy.

risks.note: BRSR material-issue risk covering structural weakness in the production network, production interruption at a single-source manufacturing site, inability to accurately predict customer demand leading to missed sales and inefficient production planning, global logistics challenges, and natural disaster or major political crisis in one or more regions. BRSR material-issue risk: the Company faces increasing regulatory complexity and operates in some geographies with inherently high corruption risks. risks.note: BRSR material-issue risk: changes in the global economic environment, financial market conditions and adverse geopolitical developments may impact the Group's revenue and profitability. risks.risk: Demand cyclicality and commoditisation pressure from customer end-markets
risks.note: Specific risks flagged include decreasing investment and delays in customers' infrastructure projects reducing steel and cement demand, customers shifting to lower-cost and more commoditised refractories because of low capacity utilisation, and lower sales volumes leading to poorer fixed-cost absorption. risks.risk: Input cost inflation, tariffs and currency exposure
risks.note: Increasing costs of core resources and supplies (energy, labour, raw materials, freight, packaging), increased trade restrictions, tariffs or export bans that could disrupt supply chains and raise material costs, and currency fluctuations affecting the cost of imports and exports. Mitigation relies on price-increase initiatives to pass inflationary costs to customers and treasury policy.

BRSR material-issue risk covering structural weakness in the production network, production interruption at a single-source manufacturing site, inability to accurately predict customer demand leading to missed sales and inefficient production planning, global logistics challenges, and natural disaster or major political crisis in one or more regions. Mitigated by geographical diversification of the production network and minimisation of sole-source materials.

Flagged with negative financial implications.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Refractory demand is directly linked to steel, cement, glass and non-ferrous metal production; steel accounts for nearly 70% of total refractory consumption in India.
- India's steelmaking capacity rose to approximately 220 MT during FY 2025-26 and remains on track towards the National Steel Policy target of 300 MT by 2030-31, with cumulative investments of approximately US$ 156 billion expected to achieve it.
- India remained the world's second-largest crude steel producer, with crude steel production of 153.6 MT and finished steel production of 146.8 MT in April 2025-February 2026, and turned a net exporter with a surplus of 0.40 MT versus a net import position in FY 2024-25.
- Indian cement production reached approximately 485 million tonnes in FY 2025-26, growing nearly 8.0%-9.0% YoY, with planned industry capital expenditure of approximately Rs 1.2-1.25 lakh crore across FY 2024-25 to FY 2026-27 toward capacity additions of nearly 130-170 MTPA; the long-term outlook for cement remains favourable through FY 2027-28.
- India's real GDP was projected to expand by approximately 7.6% in FY 2025-26, with roughly 70% of economic activity from domestic demand, supporting core industries including refractories.
- The global refractories market was valued at approximately USD 38-48 billion in 2025, with volumes rising from approximately 57 million tons in 2025 to nearly 59.6 million tons in 2026 and projected to reach around 72 million tons by 2031 at a CAGR of approximately 3.9%-4.0%; Asia-Pacific dominates the market.
- Green steel and decarbonisation momentum in India is expected to create long-term opportunities for advanced, sustainable and technology-driven refractory solutions.
- Increasing adoption of electric vehicles, renewable energy and critical metal processing is expected to further drive demand for advanced refractory solutions in the coming years.
- Headwind: the global steel industry remained under pressure from persistent overcapacity — global steelmaking capacity reached an estimated 2.6 billion metric tons by end-2025 with surplus capacity of approximately 680 million metric tons — plus weak prices, Chinese export dominance and rising trade protectionism.
- Headwind: the Indian refractory industry continues to face excess capacity, pricing pressure and increasing commoditisation of standard refractory products.
- Industrials contributed approximately 13% of RHIM India's revenues during the year, providing diversification while steel remains the largest revenue driver; the Industrial business gained market share across select segments.

Expansion during FY 2025-26 came primarily through inorganic and capability additions rather than named greenfield projects: Ashwath Technologies Private Limited became a step-down subsidiary with effect from August 1, 2025 and its integration progressed during the year, strengthening the customer base in the mini mills steel segment and enhancing offerings across slide gate systems, spare parts, refractory resale and steel flow control machinery; RHI Magnesita Seven Refractories Limited was merged into RHI Magnesita India Refractories Limited. themes.title: Refractories & metallurgical consumables
themes.need: Refractory and metallurgical-consumable makers earn recurring per-tonne pricing tied to steel/cement OUTPUT volumes - an annuity-like wear-parts thesis, not the producers own realisation cycle. Q1FY27 turned the graphite-electrode leg on PRICE rather than demand: HEG's standalone EBITDA swung from -INR 126cr in Q4FY26 to +INR 211cr at a 29% margin on LOWER volumes, entirely realisation and mix, after GrafTech announced $600-1,200/t and Tokai $930/t electrode price increases. The timing is unusually favourable - HEG's own price rises only take effect from October because its book is committed through Sept/Oct, while needle-coke inflation (+$200-300/t on 10-15% of electrode cost) hits the P&L only Nov-Jan. RAIN adds the calcined-petroleum-coke anode consumable into aluminium smelters (Carbon EBITDA up INR 1.63B as CPC prices ran $50-100 above the West on China's supply crunch); SMLT the cored-wire leg into steel mills.
themes.driver: Steel/cement output-volume growth driving per-tonne consumables demand; HEG's October price increases landing against needle-coke inflation arriving only Nov-Jan - Q3 is the quarter the margin-maintenance promise is decided.
